header.text: This text is from an article in the Somerville Herald:

contents.text: Somerville's newest restaurant, Natalie's Kitchen, serves large, healthy meals in a cozy, comfortable setting. The menu includes grilled chicken, rice and beans, and thick soups that will warm you during the winter. You won't want to leave the pleasant environment of Natalie's Kitchen.

header.text: <instructions>This text is from the point of view of a customer at the restaurant:</instructions>

contents.text: My friends and I had to wait a long time for a table at Natalie's Kitchen. We stood outside because the restaurant was so crowded. The heater was broken, so we asked to sit beside the fireplace. Then we learned it wasn't working. I can't even remember the food because I was shivering too much!
How is the customer's point of view different from the article author's?

choices.text: The customer makes the restaurant sound like a welcoming place.
The customer makes the restaurant sound cold and uncomfortable.

header.text: <instructions>This text is told from the point of view of Kylie, a kid who visited the aquarium:</instructions>

contents.text: I rush to the front of the line for the touch tank at the aquarium. I've been here a dozen times, but there's always something new to feel. contents.text: All my sister wanted for her birthday was to see this play. After waiting in line for hours, I took my money out of my pocket. You can imagine my dismay when the people in front of me got the last two tickets! The sold-out sign was hung right in my disappointed, weary face.

contents.text: Our company had been performing this play for three months. We'd all dreamed of selling out the hall, but it never happened—until last night. An hour before the curtain rose, I got the amazing news that every ticket had been sold. Surprised and excited, I ran to tell the other actors.

choices.text: Neil describes his dismay that the show is sold out.

"How much longer until we reach Oregon?" Daniel asked his father. It had been four months since they'd left Missouri with only their most important belongings. Daniel had been excited when they put everything into the wagon, but he had grown tired.
"Only a few more weeks," Daniel's father replied with a grin. "Soon, we'll be setting up our farm on Oregon's rich and fertile soil."

Daniel wanted to ask his father more questions, but he was too tired to talk. Instead, he imagined what life in Oregon would be like. Daniel pictured a flowing river, fields of corn, and trees covered with apples. Smiling, he pretended to pick one off a branch. He licked his lips and could almost taste the fruit. Daniel's steps quickened as he daydreamed about farm life. He knew Oregon would be amazing.

textContent.text: This is going to be a long day, I thought. I'd only met Mom's friend Melissa once, so I didn't understand why I had to attend this wedding. But there I was, waiting for the event to start. As guests filed into the brightly lit church, I sighed and tugged at my collar.
My mother put a hand on my shoulder and leaned closer to me. "Jeffrey, stop fiddling with your clothes, and just try to enjoy this," she said. "It's a happy occasion."

Surely I wasn't the only miserable person here. I turned to examine the other wedding guests. To my surprise, many were happily chatting, and no one seemed upset to be wearing fancy clothes. In fact, I began to sense excitement in the air. The organ played, and people oohed and aahed over the colorful bunches of flowers that decorated the church. My mom couldn't wait for the wedding to begin. I guess the happy mood caught on, because then even I started to get excited about seeing Melissa.
